newsitem.title: USA: Malaria vaccine shows promise in early test.
newsitem.headline: Malaria vaccine shows promise in early test.

text.p: U.S. Army researchers reported in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine they may have found a vaccine for the deadliest form of malaria known as plasmodium flaciparum Malaria.
This form of malaria causes more than 2 million deaths annually, according to the Wolrd Health Organisation and there is currently no effective vaccine to prevent it.

But in tests on seven volunteers injected with three doses of a vaccine known as RTS,S and then exposed to infected mosquitoes, only one developed malaria. In contrast, all six control subjects and 12 of the 15 volunteers who were given different formulations of the vaccine contracted the disease.
The most effective formulation combined RTS,S, developed by SmithKline Beecham Biologicals in Belgium, a subsidiary of SmithKline Beecham Plc, with two chemicals known to stimulate the immune system.

But the research team, led by Dr. Jose A. Stoute of the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research in Washington, warned that many important questions still had to be addressed before the full potential of the vaccine was known.

The researchers said more safety studies were needed to weed out some of the side effects, determine if the vaccine's protection was long-lasting, and to see if the concoction worked as well in the field as it seemed to in this small, preliminary study.
Based on medicine's track record with malaria, the researchers have reason to be cautious. Doctors have tried without success for years to develop a practical vaccine for the disease.

The microorganism responsible for malaria is so adept at avoiding the immune system, even people who have been naturally exposed to the parasite rarely develop complete immunity. The only vaccination strategy that has consistently worked has been to expose someone to six to 10 months worth of bites from mosquitoes that have been irradiated to cripple the parasite. But that is not practical.
Although malaria could once be treated reliably with the drug chloroquine, many parasites have developed a resistance to that medication.

Some of the RTS,S preparations seemed to have serious side effects of their own. After the second injection, there were reports of pain, fever, headache and malaise. As a result, the researchers either reduced the dose of the third injection, or skipped it altogether.
In an editorial, Drs. Ruth S. Nussenzweig and Fidel Zavala of New York University Medical Centre called the results "a considerable advance in the development of malaria vaccines."

But they warned that any proposed vaccine should be tested "among people who live in areas in which malaria is endemic, where the levels of transmission are high and there are multiple parasite strains."
